stem: At the cash break-even sales level, a project's _____ is exactly zero.
options: net income
NPV
payback period
operating cash flow
explanation: Cash break-even sets OCF = 0, so Q_C = FC/(P − v). Net income = 0 is the accounting break-even (depreciation joins the numerator) and NPV = 0 is the financial break-even.

stem: Kootenay Outfitters launches a new product line. At 9,000 units a year the line just covers its fixed operating costs in cash, but nothing is left over to repay the initial outlay. Which break-even point is this?
options: Cash break-even
Accounting break-even
Financial break-even
Payback break-even
explanation: Covering the fixed cash costs and nothing more means OCF = 0, the cash break-even Q_C = FC/(P − v). Nothing is left to recover the outlay, so the IRR is −100%. Accounting break-even would at least return the depreciation (OCF = D), and financial break-even would also earn the required return.

stem: Fraser Valley Kayaks plans a paddleboard line. The price is $64.50 per board, variable cost is $38.20 per board, fixed costs are $412,000 a year and depreciation is $165,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the cash break-even quantity (boards per year)?
solution: Contribution margin P − v = 64.50 − 38.20 = $26.30 per board
Cash break-even: OCF = 0, so Q_C = FC/(P − v) = 412,000/26.30 = 15,665.40 boards per year

errors.label: Added depreciation to the numerator
errors.explain: That is the accounting break-even. Depreciation is not a cash cost, so it stays out of the cash break-even.

errors.label: Divided fixed costs by the price
errors.explain: Each board contributes P − v = $26.30 toward fixed costs, not the whole price.

errors.label: Divided fixed costs by the variable cost
errors.explain: The denominator is the contribution margin P − v, not the variable cost per unit.

explanation: Cash break-even is the sales level where OCF = 0: Q_C = FC/(P − v). Depreciation is not a cash cost, so it plays no part (that is why the $165,000 is a distractor).

stem: Peace River Pottery sells mugs for $46.80. Each mug costs $11.35 in labour, $7.90 in clay and glaze and $1.25 in packaging. Fixed costs are $385,000 a year and depreciation is $140,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the cash break-even quantity?
options: 19,962 mugs
13,975 mugs
14,639 mugs
8,226 mugs
explanation: Total variable cost is v = 11.35 + 7.90 + 1.25 = $20.50, so P − v = $26.30 and Q_C = 385,000/26.30 = 14,639 mugs. Adding the $140,000 of depreciation gives 19,962 (the accounting break-even), and dropping packaging from v overstates the margin and understates the break-even.

stem: Algoma Canoe sells a model for $1,240 with a variable cost of $815 per canoe. The project's cash break-even is 538 canoes a year. What annual fixed costs does that imply?
solution: Q_C = FC/(P − v) rearranges to FC = Q_C × (P − v)

errors.label: Multiplied Q_C by the price
errors.explain: Only the contribution margin P − v covers fixed costs, so FC = Q_C × (P − v), not Q_C × P.

errors.label: Multiplied Q_C by the variable cost
errors.explain: That is total variable cost at the break-even volume, not the fixed costs.

errors.label: Divided Q_C by the margin
errors.explain: The formula is FC/(P − v) = Q_C, so FC is the product Q_C × (P − v), not the quotient.

explanation: Rearrange Q_C = FC/(P − v) to FC = Q_C × (P − v). At the break-even volume the total contribution exactly equals fixed costs.

stem: Okanagan Cider Works prices a new line at $58.00 a case with a variable cost of $33.50. Fixed costs are $310,000 a year and depreciation is $120,000 a year. The tax rate is 30%, and any tax loss on this project can be used against the firm's other income. At what quantity is OCF exactly zero?
solution: OCF = [(P − v)Q − FC](1 − T) + T·D; set OCF = 0

errors.label: Subtracted T·D but did not divide by (1 − T)
errors.explain: The shield sits after tax while the numerator is pre-tax, so it must be grossed up by 1/(1 − T).

errors.label: Ignored taxes: FC/(P − v)
errors.explain: With taxes the depreciation shield still produces cash when the pre-tax result is negative, which lowers the cash break-even.

errors.label: Added the grossed-up shield instead of subtracting it
errors.explain: At OCF = 0 the shield replaces some of the fixed cost burden, so it is subtracted from FC.

explanation: With taxes, OCF = [(P − v)Q − FC](1 − T) + T·D. Setting it to zero gives Q_C = {FC − T·D/(1 − T)}/(P − v) = 10,553.94, below FC/(P − v) = 12,653.06 because the depreciation tax shield is still earned when pre-tax profit is negative.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts cash break-even with accounting break-even?
options: Cash break-even includes the required return on the investment; accounting break-even does not
Cash break-even leaves depreciation out of the numerator; accounting break-even includes it
Cash break-even is the higher of the two quantities for a project with positive depreciation
Cash break-even sets net income to zero; accounting break-even sets operating cash flow to zero
explanation: Q_C = FC/(P − v) covers only cash fixed costs; Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) also covers depreciation, so Q_A > Q_C. The required return belongs to financial break-even, and the claim that cash break-even sets net income to zero swaps the roles of net income and OCF.

stem: Which statement about a project operating exactly at its cash break-even point is NOT true?
options: Operating cash flow is zero in every year
The IRR is −100%
The payback period equals the project's life
The NPV equals minus the initial outlay
explanation: At cash break-even no cash comes back, so the project never pays back, the IRR is −100% and NPV = −I0. Payback exactly equal to the life describes the accounting break-even, where OCF = D.

stem: Why is the cash break-even quantity always below the accounting break-even quantity when a project has positive depreciation?
options: Cash break-even uses the after-tax contribution margin, which is larger
Cash break-even discounts the fixed costs, which makes the numerator smaller
Cash break-even leaves out variable costs, which makes the denominator larger
Depreciation is not a cash cost, so cash break-even only has to cover the cash fixed costs
explanation: Q_A adds D to the numerator, and D is an accounting charge rather than a cash outflow. Discounting enters only the financial break-even (and raises it), and variable costs sit in the denominator of all three.

stem: Tri-City Print's new line has a cash break-even of 8,000 units a year, and management forecasts sales of 7,400 units. What does this tell management?
options: Operating cash flow is negative, so the line needs cash just to keep running
Net income is zero, so the line earns its depreciation in cash
NPV is zero, so the line earns exactly its required return
The line pays back its outlay in exactly its useful life
explanation: Sales below Q_C mean (P − v)Q < FC, so OCF < 0. That is worse than the accounting break-even case, where OCF at least equals depreciation. Zero NPV and payback equal to life describe other break-even points.

stem: Lakeland Foods has spare capacity. A one-time order for 5,000 jars is offered at $2.60 a jar. Variable cost is $2.05 a jar, the $480,000 of fixed costs is paid whether or not the order is accepted, and the average cost is $3.10 a jar. What should it do?
options: Reject: $2.60 is below the average cost of $3.10 a jar
Accept: the $0.55 contribution per jar adds $2,750 to cash flow and fixed costs are paid anyway
Reject: the order must also cover its share of the $480,000 of fixed costs
Accept only if the price exceeds $3.10, so the order shows an accounting profit
explanation: Fixed costs are effectively sunk for this choice, so only the marginal cost (v = $2.05) matters: 5,000 × (2.60 − 2.05) = $2,750 of extra cash. Average cost includes fixed costs that do not change, which is why it misleads.

stem: In Q_C = FC/(P − v), fixed costs rise by 20% and the contribution margin P − v also rises by 20%. What happens to the cash break-even quantity?
options: It rises by 20%
It rises by 44%
It is unchanged
It falls by 20%
explanation: Both the numerator and the denominator are multiplied by 1.20, so Q_C = 1.20 FC/(1.20 (P − v)) is unchanged. A 20% rise in only FC would lift Q_C by 20%, and a 44% rise has no basis in the formula.

stem: When taxes are ignored, a project's cash break-even quantity does not depend on its depreciation.
options: True
False
explanation: Q_C = FC/(P − v) has no D in it. Depreciation affects the accounting break-even Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v), not the cash break-even.

stem: Mapleview Bikes' project has fixed costs of $1,020,000 a year and a variable cost of $310 per bike. At a price of $480 its cash break-even is 6,000 bikes. If the price is raised to $520 with costs unchanged, what is the new cash break-even?
options: 4,857 bikes
1,962 bikes
4,588 bikes
5,538 bikes
explanation: The contribution margin rises from $170 to $210, so Q_C = 1,020,000/210 = 4,857 bikes. Dividing by the whole price (1,962) ignores variable cost, cutting 6,000 by the 23.5% rise in the margin (4,588) treats Q_C as linear in the margin, and scaling 6,000 by the price ratio (5,538) treats Q_C as proportional to 1/P. Q_C = FC/(P − v) must be recomputed with the new margin.

stem: At the accounting break-even sales level, a project's _____ is exactly zero.
options: operating cash flow
NPV
net income
payback period
explanation: Accounting break-even sets net income (and so EBIT and taxes) to zero: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v). Operating cash flow equals depreciation at that point, not zero.

stem: At 4,600 units a year the income statement of a new line shows EBIT of zero, no taxes and net income of zero, while operating cash flow equals the annual depreciation. Which break-even point is this?
options: Cash break-even
Financial break-even
Payback break-even
Accounting break-even
explanation: Net income = 0 defines accounting break-even. Since OCF = NI + D, OCF = D there, which is positive; at cash break-even OCF would be zero and at financial break-even NPV would be zero.

stem: Cariboo Trailers will invest $2,640,000 in equipment, depreciated straight-line to zero over 8 years. Fixed costs are $845,000 a year, the price is $31.40 per unit and variable cost is $18.65 per unit. Ignoring taxes, what is the accounting break-even quantity (units per year)?

errors.label: Left depreciation out (used FC only)
errors.explain: That is the cash break-even. Accounting break-even must cover depreciation too.

errors.label: Added the whole investment instead of one year's depreciation
errors.explain: Only the annual charge D = I0/N belongs in the numerator.

errors.label: Divided by the price instead of P − v
errors.explain: The denominator is the contribution margin P − v, not the price.

explanation: Accounting break-even is where net income is zero: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) with D = I0/N for straight-line to zero. Taxes do not matter because taxable income is zero there.

stem: Yellowhead Signage plans a project with price $27.50, variable cost $16.20 and fixed costs of $520,000 a year. It needs a $1,350,000 investment, depreciated straight-line to zero over 6 years. The required return is 10%; ignore taxes. If sales sit exactly at the accounting break-even each year, what is the NPV?

errors.label: Treated zero profit as zero NPV
errors.explain: Accounting break-even makes net income zero, but the investment is only recovered with no return, so NPV is negative.

errors.label: Set OCF to zero (cash break-even)
errors.explain: At accounting break-even OCF equals depreciation, not zero; the flows of $225,000 are still worth something.

errors.label: Used a 5-year annuity factor
errors.explain: The project lasts 6 years, so the annuity factor must use N = 6.

explanation: At accounting break-even OCF = D = I0/N each year, so NPV = I0[(1/N) × annuity factor − 1]. With any positive required return that is negative: the project returns the money invested but never the time value (IRR = 0%).

stem: Yukon Snowmobile Parts has a price of $212 and a variable cost of $139 per unit. Fixed costs are $1,460,000 a year. It invests $5,600,000 in equipment, depreciated straight-line to zero over 7 years, and expects operating cash flow of $1,200,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the accounting break-even quantity?
options: 36,438 units
20,000 units
30,959 units
96,712 units
explanation: D = 5,600,000/7 = $800,000, so Q_A = (1,460,000 + 800,000)/73 = 30,959 units. The $1,200,000 of operating cash flow is a lure: at accounting break-even OCF equals D, not the base-case OCF. Using FC alone gives the cash break-even and using the whole investment overstates the charge.

stem: A project must reach accounting break-even at 12,500 units a year. Fixed costs are $288,000, depreciation is $96,000 and variable cost is $14.80 per unit. What selling price achieves that?
explanation: Solve Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) for P: P = (FC + D)/Q_A + v = 384,000/12,500 + 14.80 = $45.52. Leaving out v gives only the contribution margin of $30.72, omitting D lowers the price to $37.84, and subtracting v moves the wrong way.

stem: Prairie Window Systems has a price of $410, variable cost of $268, fixed costs of $390,000 and depreciation of $150,000 a year; the tax rate is 32%. Use OCF = NI + D at the break-even, then Q = {FC + (OCF − T·D)/(1 − T)}/(P − v), to find the accounting break-even quantity.
solution: NI = 0 at accounting break-even, so OCF = NI + D = $150,000
Q_A = 540,000/142 = 3,802.82 units, identical to (FC + D)/(P − v)

errors.label: Divided the margin by (1 − T) as well
errors.explain: No tax is paid at accounting break-even, so there is nothing to gross up in the denominator.

errors.label: Used after-tax depreciation D(1 − T)
errors.explain: Depreciation is a pre-tax charge in the break-even condition; the shield was already handled by the general formula.

errors.label: Multiplied the whole numerator by (1 − T)
errors.explain: At zero profit the tax rate cancels completely, so the numerator is just FC + D.

explanation: Because OCF = D at accounting break-even, (OCF − T·D)/(1 − T) = D(1 − T)/(1 − T) = D, so Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) whatever the tax rate. The tax rate is a distractor.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts accounting break-even with financial break-even?
options: Accounting break-even charges the opportunity cost of capital; financial break-even does not
Accounting break-even sets net income to zero and ignores the time value of money; financial sets NPV to zero
Accounting break-even is always higher than financial break-even, because depreciation is included
The two are equal whenever the project has no salvage value
explanation: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) recovers the investment with no return, while Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v) uses the OCF* that earns the required return, so for a normal project Q_F > Q_A.

stem: Which statement about a project operating exactly at its accounting break-even point is NOT true?
options: Net income is zero
Taxes paid are zero
The project's NPV is zero
Operating cash flow equals depreciation
explanation: At accounting break-even EBIT, taxes and net income are zero and OCF = NI + D = D. The investment comes back with no return (IRR = 0%), so NPV is negative at any positive required return.

stem: Why is clearing the accounting break-even not enough to justify accepting a project?
options: It counts depreciation as a cash outflow, which makes NPV look worse than it is
It includes interest expense, which does not belong in project cash flows
It ignores variable costs, so the quantity it gives is too low
At accounting break-even the IRR is zero, so NPV is negative at any positive required return
explanation: Accounting break-even earns only the depreciation back (OCF = D, payback equal to the life). Without a return on the money tied up, NPV = I0[(1/N) × annuity factor − 1] < 0. That is why we also need the financial break-even.

stem: Muskoka Skiff Co. finds an accounting break-even of 44 skiffs a year against a sales forecast of 58. A director says, "We clear break-even by 14 skiffs, so the project is safe." What is the best response?
options: Clearing accounting break-even says nothing about NPV, so compute the financial break-even
Agree: any project forecast above accounting break-even has a positive NPV
Agree: above accounting break-even the IRR must exceed the required return
Disagree: the project must still reach its cash break-even before it is safe
explanation: Sales above Q_A keep net income positive, but the IRR only exceeds zero, not necessarily the required return. Since Q_F > Q_A, a forecast of 58 skiffs could still fall short of Q_F. Cash break-even is lower than Q_A, so clearing Q_A already clears it.

stem: Which change would lower a project's accounting break-even quantity, all else equal?
options: Buying more equipment that raises straight-line depreciation
A cut in annual fixed costs
A lower selling price
A higher variable cost per unit
explanation: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v): smaller FC shrinks the numerator, while more depreciation raises it and a lower P or higher v shrinks the contribution margin in the denominator.

stem: A pricier machine adds $50,000 to annual straight-line depreciation. Fixed cash costs and the contribution margin of $12.50 per unit are unchanged. What happens to the break-even quantities?
options: Q_A rises by 4,000 units and Q_C rises by 4,000 units
Q_A falls by 4,000 units and Q_C is unchanged
Q_A rises by 4,000 units and Q_C is unchanged
Both are unchanged, because depreciation is not a cash cost
explanation: ΔQ_A = ΔD/(P − v) = 50,000/12.50 = 4,000 units, and it is a rise because D sits in the numerator. Q_C = FC/(P − v) contains no depreciation, so it is unchanged. Depreciation does matter to Q_A even though it is not a cash cost.

stem: For a project depreciated straight-line to zero, operating at its accounting break-even every year gives a payback period equal to the project's life and an IRR of zero.
options: True
False
explanation: At accounting break-even OCF = D = I0/N each year, so the cash flows add up to exactly I0 over N years: payback = N and IRR = 0%.

stem: Algonquin Candles sells candles at $18.50 with a variable cost of $7.25 each. Fixed costs are $196,000 a year and depreciation is $59,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what annual sales revenue is needed to reach the accounting break-even?

errors.label: Used the cash break-even quantity
errors.explain: That leaves depreciation out; the accounting break-even must cover FC + D.

errors.label: Reported total contribution (FC + D) as revenue
errors.explain: FC + D is the contribution needed, not the sales revenue; revenue is P × Q_A.

errors.label: Multiplied the quantity by the variable cost
errors.explain: Revenue is quantity × price, not quantity × variable cost.

explanation: Find Q_A first, then convert to dollars with the price. At revenue of $419,333.33, variable costs are $164,333.33, fixed costs $196,000 and depreciation $59,000: EBIT = 0.

stem: Why does the tax rate not appear in Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v)?
options: Taxes are paid only on cash flows, and operating cash flow is zero at that point
Net income is zero there, so no tax is paid and the rate drops out
Taxes are already included in the fixed costs FC
The depreciation tax shield exactly cancels tax on revenue at every sales level
explanation: Net income = (S − VC − FC − D)(1 − T) = 0 requires S − VC − FC − D = 0 whatever T is, so dividing by (1 − T) removes it. At that point OCF = D, not zero.

stem: A project has an accounting break-even of 4,400 units a year, a price of $85, a variable cost of $52 and fixed costs of $90,000 a year. Its equipment is depreciated straight-line to zero over 5 years. What initial investment does this imply?

steps.label: Annual depreciation D = Q_A(P − v) − FC

solution: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) rearranges to D = Q_A(P − v) − FC

errors.label: Did not subtract fixed costs when solving for D
errors.explain: The break-even quantity covers FC + D, so D is what is left after fixed costs.

errors.label: Reported one year's depreciation as the investment
errors.explain: Straight-line depreciation is I0/N, so the investment is N times the annual charge.

explanation: Work backwards: D = Q_A(P − v) − FC = $55,200, and with straight-line depreciation to zero over 5 years the investment is I0 = 5D = $276,000.
